title: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis

steps.tx: Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis most frequently involves the **superior sagittal sinus** and transverse sinuses, presenting with headache, progressive **papilloedema**, focal neurological deficits, and seizures. Elevated cerebral venous pressure impairs cerebrospinal fluid absorption at arachnoid villi, producing severe intracranial hypertension that mimics pseudotumour cerebri in subacute presentations.

right.title: Deep Venous System

steps.tx: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography and **MR venography** establish definitive diagnosis by demonstrating the pathognomonic **empty delta sign** within the dural venous sinuses. This hallmark sign represents a central non-enhancing intraluminal thrombus bounded by brightly enhancing collateral venous channels within the dura mater.

steps.tx: Bilateral parasagittal frontal and parietal **hemorrhagic infarctions** crossing conventional arterial vascular territories are virtually pathognomonic for extensive **superior sagittal sinus** thrombosis. Venous hypertension causes progressive capillary hydrostatic breakdown, extravasation of red blood cells, and subsequent cortical venous infarction with focal motor deficits.

rows: Bilateral frontal and parietal hemorrhagic infarcts

steps.tx: Bilateral thalamic and basal ganglia congestion or hemorrhagic infarction indicates deep cerebral venous system thrombosis involving the **straight sinus** and **internal cerebral veins**. Patients rapidly decline into stupor, coma, and progressive decerebrate posturing from bilateral diencephalic swelling and severe downward transtentorial herniation through tentorial incisura.

left.title: Deep Venous Occlusion
points: Internal cerebral veins and straight sinus

right.title: Superficial Venous Occlusion
points: Prominent motor seizures and focal deficits
Higher rate of complete neurological recovery

steps.tx: Therapeutic anticoagulation with weight-adjusted low-molecular-weight **heparin** or unfractionated heparin is the first-line treatment for acute cerebral **venous thrombosis** even in the presence of baseline hemorrhagic infarction. Prompt anticoagulation halts progressive thrombus propagation, restores collateral cerebral venous outflow, and facilitates endogenous fibrinolysis without increasing intracranial haematoma expansion.

steps.tx: Following acute parenteral stabilization, maintenance **oral anticoagulation** is continued for **3** to **6** months in transiently provoked thrombosis, and extended to **12** months or lifelong for unprovoked cases or severe hereditary **thrombophilia**. Direct oral anticoagulants or vitamin K antagonists provide sustained protection against systemic and cerebral venous recurrence.

steps.tx: **Cavernous sinus thrombosis** commonly arises from retrograde septic thrombophlebitis tracking from facial furuncles or paranasal infections, presenting with chemosis, severe **proptosis**, ophthalmoplegia, and sensory loss in the V1 and V2 divisions. High-dose intravenous antimicrobial therapy targeting Staphylococcus aureus and urgent surgical sinus drainage are paramount to prevent bilateral cavernous sinus involvement.

left.title: Cavernous Sinus Features
points: Ophthalmoplegia of CN III, IV, and VI
Sensory deficit across V1 and V2 dermatomes
Rapid contralateral spread across circular sinus

right.title: Emergency Management
points: Surgical drainage of primary paranasal focus

steps.tx: Endovascular **mechanical thrombectomy** or catheter-directed local thrombolysis serves as vital rescue intervention for patients who experience progressive **neurological deterioration** despite therapeutic heparinization. Direct endovascular aspiration extracts bulky occlusive dural thrombi, rapidly relieves intractable venous congestion, and averts impending fatal transtentorial brain herniation in critical care settings.
